newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS - MAY 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS - MAY 21.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--The government is expected to make decisions on the four trillion drachmas arms procurements programme within the next few days with sources saying the contract to upgrade the air force's F-4 fighter plances will be placed with US firm Rockwell, whose bid was nine billion drachmas cheaper that Germany's DASA. Negotiations on the purchase of a Dutch frigate and US Patriot missile systems are in their final stages.

--The construction of the new Acropolis Museum was approved last night by the Central Archaeological Council, following a number of revisions to the original design by Italian architects Pazarelli and Nikoletti.

--Eight months after the announcement by Education Minister Gerasimos Arsenis of far-reaching reforms to the education system, the changes are still "academic" with little progress having been made and charges now that school textbooks will not be ready for the new school year in September.

--The death of a Greek policeman stationed at the Greek consulate general in Gjirokaster yesterday has drawn a wealth of rumours that he was murdered. Official sources however insist that Nikos Markakis died while cleaning his gun and becoming entangled with his glasses.
--A church educational consultant has recommended schools not teach the works of Nikos Kazantzakis (Zorba the Greek, The Last Temptation of Christ) calling the author anti-Christian and perverted.

--The OECD is expected to recommend in its forthcoming report that the pension age be increased along with contributions or Greece will be faced with the prospect of the social security system collapsing under the weight of deficits.
--Proposals to legalise soft drugs, such as marijuana, and even allow production for personal use have caused a furore in some quarters.
--A new bill submitted to Parliament is expected to make changes to new pensions in the public sector and in the seamen's pension fund NAT.
--Fine arts students in Thessaloniki protested yesterday at the lack of buildings that would allow them to register for studies.
